Welcome to The Internet of Compromised Things - Your router can be used to attack all the computers connected to it.
It's always some near-useless feature that nobody uses which causes these exploits.

For all meaningful traffic sent through a compromised router that isn't HTTPS encrypted, it is 100% game over

That's the point: you shouldn't be downloading Chrome without HTTPS. It's inherently unsafe. Don't be surprised when data sent over http is manipulated in-flight.

Attacks on the router are a non-issue: everything you don't want intercepted, sniffed on or modified should already be sent over https (or another encrypted protocol). That's the thing we have to fix: use https everywhere. We can't secure every point our data travels through, but we can secure the data.

Exactly this. The basis of the Internet wasn't originally designed to be inherently secure. It was a communication tool for a handful of groups connected via what amounted to a smallish WAN. Protocols like HTTPS were introduced when it was realized that we needed to actually protect the data floating past countless devices that could easily read the data in-transit.

The HTTPS Everywhere browser extension has been around for a while and can be used to help fix this problem.
